newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss suspect foreign agenda for wartime review.
newsitem.headline: Swiss suspect foreign agenda for wartime review.

text.p: Stunned by virulent attacks from abroad about Switzerland's wartime links to Nazi Germany, Swiss officials and commentators have started accusing foreign competitors of expressly campaigning to discredit the country.

Politicians and newspapers suggest that foreigners jealous of Swiss financial prowess or in need of a political boost are exploiting the drive for a review of Swiss-Nazi financial deals and a fresh search for Holocaust victims' unclaimed wealth.

Few doubt the wisdom of launching such an inquest to lay to rest any lingering doubts over the whereabouts of looted Nazi gold or Jewish assets, but whether this is to assuage Swiss consciences or to counter foreign detractors remains disputed.

"The National Council stands up to Senator D'Amato. There will be a probe, but done calmly," was the headline on Tuesday's Journal de Geneve after the lower house of parliament backed a sweeping historical probe of Swiss wartime history.
It was referring to New York Senator Alfonse D'Amato, who has taken a well-publicised interest in the Swiss National Bank's purchases of Nazi gold and the search for potential Holocaust accounts.

D'Amato has called for re-negotiating the 1946 Washington Agreement, in which Switzerland agreed to pay 250 million Swiss francs in compensation for wartime purchases of gold that the Nazis looted from conquered nations or stole from Jews.
Many Swiss were outraged that D'Amato would even suggest reopening a 50-year-old accord, but the U.S. embassy in Berne refused to rule this out.

"The State Department and the American embassy share the senator's desire for a thorough and transparent review of dormant accounts of Holocaust victims and Nazi assets in Swiss financial insitutions," an embassy statement said on Tuesday.
"Yet a careful evaluation may take some time," it added.

Foreign meddling came under fire on Monday when the National Council backed a government decree to lift strict bank secrecy and let a panel of historians and experts probe whether neutral Switzerland acted honourably during and after the war.
"It is no coincidence that especially harsh tones are coming from the City of London or the New York senatorial campaign," charged Marc Suter, a deputy from the Radical Democratic Party.

"One reason this storm of indignation is roaring through the Anglo-Saxon newspapers may be to weaken Switzerland as a financial centre, to undermine Swiss banking secrecy or to deflect attention from their own shortcomings," he said.
The influential business paper Finanz und Wirtschaft raised the same point in its weekend edition.

"Certain circles are using the tragic fate of Holocaust victims to discredit the (still) extant advantage Switzerland as a financial centre and its banks have in global competition," it wrote, citing Swiss strength in private banking and asset management.

"Leading Swiss banks' standing in international asset management encourages envy. These envious people, who are skilfully using attacks on Switzerland to weaken the banking centre's reputation, must be faced now, and not in five years when the historical investigation may be available," it added.
Swiss officials take umbrage at the suggestion that only outside pressure led to the historical review, which has won practically unstoppable political momentum.
"For many this comes late, too late, but we are not starting from scratch," Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti told the debate, calling for more "honesty" from Switzerland's foreign critics.
He recalled the way Switzerland froze German assets after the war, handed over Nazi wealth to the Allies and hunted Holocaust accounts as early as 1962.
